candidates.source_name: 1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) / Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36)
candidates.draft_body:
1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36) (c. 200 BC)

The angel Michael explains the mountain on which the tree of life grows: 'This high mountain which thou hast seen, whose summit is like the throne of God, is His throne, where the Holy Great One, the Lord of Glory, the Eternal King, will sit, when He shall come down to visit the earth with goodness' — the throne-mountain of the eschatological visitation. The mountain serves simultaneously as God's throne AND as the place of His descent to creation: in the eschaton the transcendent and immanent are reunited geographically. Tewahedo theological geography preserves this throne-mountain imagery; Mount Zion (and by extension every consecrated church building) participates in this eschatological throne-mountain typology.

candidates.source_name: 1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) / Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36)
candidates.draft_body:
1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36) (c. 200 BC)

Of the tree of life at the eschaton: 'Its fruit shall be for food to the elect: it shall be transplanted to the holy place, to the temple of the Lord, the Eternal King' — the transplantation of the tree to the eschatological temple. The tree of life is not merely restored to its Edenic location but UPGRADED to the temple of God Himself: the original garden setting becomes the new-creation sanctuary. Tewahedo liturgical theology reads this as the textual basis for the consecrated altar table as participation in the eschatological temple-tree: the eucharistic bread received at the altar IS the fruit of the eschatological tree of life given proleptically.
